---
title: "Regression Adjustment for Relative and Ratio Effects"
format:
  html:
    link-external-newwindow: true
---

This note combines regression adjustment with the uniformly valid procedures developed for relative treatment effects and ratio metrics.
We use the regression-adjusted treatment-group means and confidence intervals from the [variance reduction via regression note](../regression/) in place of their unadjusted counterparts.
Unless stated otherwise, we retain that note's model, notation, and assumptions.

# Relative treatment effects {#sec-regression-relative-treatment-effects}

The [relative treatment effects note](../lift/) constructs uniformly asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the ATE scaled by the absolute value of the control mean.
In this section, we adapt the construction for regression adjustment by replacing the treatment-group means with their regression-adjusted counterparts.

For this section, restrict $\Theta$ so that $\overline y_{0,n}\neq0$ for every $n$.
Define

$$
\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE}}
=
\overline y_{1,n}-\overline y_{0,n},
\qquad
\rho_n
=
\frac{\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE}}}{|\overline y_{0,n}|}.
$$ {#eq-regression-relative-treatment-effect}

The regression-adjusted ATE and relative-treatment-effect estimators are

$$
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}
=
\widehat y_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}},
\qquad
\widehat\rho_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}}
{|\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|},
$$ {#eq-regression-relative-treatment-effect-estimator}

where $\widehat\rho_n^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is defined whenever $\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\neq0$.

## Regression-adjusted Fieller sets

Let $m^+=1$ and $m^-=-1$, and define

$$
\rho_n^s
=
m^s\frac{\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE}}}{\overline y_{0,n}},
\qquad
s\in\{+,-\}.
$$ {#eq-regression-sign-specific-relative-treatment-effects}

At the true value of $\rho_n^s$,

$$
\left(\rho_n^s+m^s\right)\overline y_{0,n}
-m^s\overline y_{1,n}
=
\rho_n^s\overline y_{0,n}
-m^s\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE}}
=0.
$$ {#eq-regression-sign-specific-zero-contrast}

For a candidate value $r$, replacing the treatment-group means in this contrast with the regression-adjusted treatment-group means gives

$$
r\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-m^s\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}.
$$

The corresponding coefficient vector is $(r+m^s,-m^s)'$.
Since $|r+m^s|=|1+m^sr|$, its feasible conservative standard deviation is

$$
\left|1+m^sr\right|\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\widehat\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}.
$$

We therefore define the sign-specific regression-adjusted Fieller set by

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}
=
\Bigg\{r\in\mathbb R:{}&
\left|
r\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-m^s\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}
\right|
\\
&\leq
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt n}
\left(
\left|1+m^sr\right|\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\widehat\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)
\Bigg\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-sign-specific-fieller-set}

Equivalently, squaring both sides and collecting terms gives the piecewise-quadratic form

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}
=
\Bigg\{r\in\mathbb R:{}&
\left[
\left(\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
-\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^2}{n}
\left(\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
\right]r^2
\\
&\quad-
2m^s\left[
\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}
+\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^2}{n}
\left(\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
\right]r
\\
&\quad-
\frac{2z_{1-\alpha/2}^2}{n}
\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\widehat\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\left(\left|1+m^sr\right|-1\right)
\\
&\quad+
\left(\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}\right)^2
-\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^2}{n}
\left(
\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\widehat\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)^2
\leq0
\Bigg\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-sign-specific-fieller-set-piecewise-quadratic}

At $r=\rho_n^s$, this set inverts the regression confidence interval for the contrast in (-@eq-regression-sign-specific-zero-contrast).
Therefore the [regression confidence-interval coverage result](../regression/#eq-regression-confidence-interval-coverage) implies

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left(
\rho_n^s\in C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}
\right)
\geq
1-\alpha,
\qquad s\in\{+,-\}.
$$ {#eq-regression-sign-specific-fieller-coverage}

## Connected confidence intervals

$C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}$ is a bounded interval if and only if the adjusted control mean is statistically distinguishable from zero at level $\alpha$.
To state this condition and the corresponding ATE sign test, define

$$
T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{\sqrt n\,\widehat y_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}},
\qquad
T_{\mathrm{ATE},n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{\sqrt n\,\widehat\psi_n^{\mathrm{ATE,reg}}}
{\widehat\sigma_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\widehat\sigma_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-relative-treatment-effect-statistics}

Then

$$
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}
\text{ is bounded}
\iff
\left|T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right|>z_{1-\alpha/2}.
$$ {#eq-regression-fieller-boundedness}

First suppose the sign of $\overline y_{0,n}$ is known.
Then $m^s=\operatorname{sgn}(\overline y_{0,n})$ and $\rho_n=\rho_n^s$.
Choose $\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},\alpha^{\mathrm{ATE}}>0$ such that

$$
\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}+\alpha^{\mathrm{ATE}}=\alpha,
\qquad
\alpha^{\mathrm{ATE}}\leq\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}.
$$

Define

$$
I_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}
=
\begin{cases}
C_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},n}^{\mathrm{reg},s},
& |T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|>z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}/2}, \\[3ex]
C_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}\cap[0,\infty),
& |T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}/2},
\quad T_{\mathrm{ATE},n}^{\mathrm{reg}}>z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{ATE}}/2}, \\[3ex]
C_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}\cap(-\infty,0],
& |T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}/2},
\quad T_{\mathrm{ATE},n}^{\mathrm{reg}}<-z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{ATE}}/2}, \\[3ex]
\mathbb R,
& |T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}/2},
\quad |T_{\mathrm{ATE},n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{ATE}}/2}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-regression-known-sign-relative-treatment-effect-interval}

This is the regression analogue of the [known-sign interval](../lift/#known-baseline-sign).
If the sign-specific Fieller set covers $\rho_n$, truncation can exclude $\rho_n$ only when the ATE sign test selects the wrong sign.
Applying the [regression confidence-interval coverage result](../regression/#eq-regression-confidence-interval-coverage) to the coefficient vectors $(\rho_n^s+m^s,-m^s)'$ and $(-1,1)'$ therefore gives

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left(
\rho_n\in I_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg},s}
\right)
\geq
1-\alpha.
$$ {#eq-regression-known-sign-relative-treatment-effect-coverage}

Now suppose the sign of $\overline y_{0,n}$ is unknown.
Choose $\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},\alpha_0>0$ such that

$$
\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}+\alpha_0=\alpha,
\qquad
\alpha_0\leq\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},
$$

and define

$$
I_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\begin{cases}
C_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},n}^{\mathrm{reg},+},
& T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}>z_{1-\alpha_0/2}, \\[1ex]
C_{1-\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}},n}^{\mathrm{reg},-},
& T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}<-z_{1-\alpha_0/2}, \\[1ex]
\mathbb R,
& |T_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha_0/2}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-regression-unknown-sign-relative-treatment-effect-interval}

The condition $\alpha_0\leq\alpha^{\mathrm{Fieller}}$ and (-@eq-regression-fieller-boundedness) ensure that either selected sign-specific set is bounded.
An incorrect sign selection is contained in the failure event for the regression confidence interval for $\overline y_{0,n}$, which uses coefficient vector $(1,0)'$.
On the event that the correct sign is selected, noncoverage requires the corresponding sign-specific Fieller set to miss.
Consequently, the [regression confidence-interval coverage result](../regression/#eq-regression-confidence-interval-coverage) and (-@eq-regression-sign-specific-fieller-coverage) give

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left(
\rho_n\in I_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)
\geq
1-\alpha.
$$ {#eq-regression-unknown-sign-relative-treatment-effect-coverage}

Thus the regression-adjusted construction preserves the uniform coverage of the original Fieller procedure while replacing the unadjusted arm variances with weakly smaller projection-residual variances.

# Ratio metrics {#sec-regression-ratio-metrics}

The [ratio metrics note](../ratio/) studies differences between treatment-group ratios using Fieller, delta-method, and hybrid confidence intervals.
To combine those methods with regression adjustment, we first extend the regression setup to a pair of outcomes.

## Bivariate regression setup

Suppose that each unit has observed numerator and denominator outcomes $(Y_i,Z_i)$, with potential outcomes $(y_{i,d},z_{i,d})$ under treatment group $d\in\{0,1\}$.
Both outcomes satisfy the observation equation in [Assumption 2'](../ratio/#asm-sutva).
Apply [the regression projection](../regression/#eq-regression-projection-residuals) separately to the numerator and denominator potential outcomes, and denote the resulting coefficients and residuals by

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_{i,d,n}^{y,\mathrm{reg}}
&=
y_{i,d}-\overline y_{d,n}
-\left(\boldsymbol w_i-\overline{\boldsymbol w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}^y,
\\[1ex]
u_{i,d,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
&=
z_{i,d}-\overline z_{d,n}
-\left(\boldsymbol w_i-\overline{\boldsymbol w}_n\right)'
\boldsymbol\beta_{d,n}^z.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-projection-residuals}

Collect the two residuals and define their within-treatment-group covariance matrix by

$$
\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
u_{i,d,n}^{y,\mathrm{reg}} \\
u_{i,d,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\left(\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)'.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-residual-covariance}

Throughout this section, redefine the parameter configuration as

$$
\boldsymbol\theta
=
\left(
p,
\{y_{i,0},z_{i,0}\}_{i=1}^\infty,
\{y_{i,1},z_{i,1}\}_{i=1}^\infty,
\{\boldsymbol w_i\}_{i=1}^\infty
\right),
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-parameter}

and let $\Theta$ denote the corresponding parameter space.

For this section, replace parts (i) and (ii) of [Assumption 3''](../regression/#asm-regression-covariates) with their multivariate counterparts: $\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is positive definite for every $d\in\{0,1\}$, $\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta$, and all sufficiently large $n$, and

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\max_{1\leq i\leq n}
\frac{
\left(\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)'
\left(\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^{-1}
\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
}{n}
=0,
\qquad d\in\{0,1\}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-maximum-variance-share}

Part (iii), the maximum-leverage condition, remains unchanged.

Apply the fully interacted regression separately to $Y_i$ and $Z_i$.
Denote the resulting treatment-group intercepts by $\widehat y_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$, and collect the corresponding fitted residuals as

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol U}_{i,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat U_{i,n}^{y,\mathrm{reg}} \\
\widehat U_{i,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Define the within-treatment-group fitted-residual covariance matrix by

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{1}{N_{d,n}}
\sum_{i=1}^n
D_{i,d}
\widehat{\boldsymbol U}_{i,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol U}_{i,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)'.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-fitted-residual-covariance}

For a candidate ratio $r\in\mathbb R$, define the population projected mean, its regression estimator, and its fitted-residual standard deviation by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overline v_{d,n}(r)
&=
\overline y_{d,n}-r\overline z_{d,n},
\\[1ex]
\widehat v_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)
&=
\widehat y_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-r\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}},
\\[1ex]
\left\{\widehat\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)\right\}^2
&=
\frac{\overline D_{1-d,n}}{\overline D_{d,n}}
\begin{pmatrix}1&-r\end{pmatrix}
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-r\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-projected-quantities}

Linearity of least squares implies that $\widehat v_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)$ and $\widehat U_{i,n}^{y,\mathrm{reg}}-r\widehat U_{i,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}$ are exactly the intercept and fitted residual obtained by regressing $Y_i-rZ_i$ on the fully interacted design.
Moreover, the Rayleigh-quotient inequality gives

$$
\frac{
\left(u_{i,d,n}^{y,\mathrm{reg}}-r u_{i,d,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
}{
n
\begin{pmatrix}1&-r\end{pmatrix}
\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-r\end{pmatrix}
}
\leq
\frac{
\left(\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)'
\left(\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^{-1}
\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
}{n}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-rayleigh-bound}

Thus (-@eq-regression-ratio-maximum-variance-share) supplies the scalar maximum-variance-share condition uniformly over $r$.
Applying the [regression coverage argument](../regression/#eq-regression-confidence-interval-coverage) along arbitrary sequences of parameters and candidate ratios and then arguing by contradiction gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\inf_{r\in\mathbb R}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\Bigg(
\left|
\widehat v_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)
-\overline v_{d,n}(r)
\right|
&\leq
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt n}
\widehat\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)
\Bigg)
\geq
1-\alpha,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-uniform-projected-coverage}

for each $d\in\{0,1\}$.
This is the regression analogue of the [uniform projected-outcome coverage result](../ratio/#eq-uniform-projected-coverage){.quarto-xref}.

On an outcome for which a required treatment-group regression or standard deviation is undefined, interpret every confidence set in this section as $\mathbb R$.
This convention can only increase coverage and avoids assigning values to intermediate ratios on exceptional outcomes.

## Fieller difference confidence interval

Assume $\overline z_{d,n}\neq0$ for every $n$ and $d\in\{0,1\}$, and define

$$
r_{d,n}
=
\frac{\overline y_{d,n}}{\overline z_{d,n}},
\qquad
r_n
=
r_{1,n}-r_{0,n}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-treatment-effect}

Because $\overline v_{d,n}(r_{d,n})=0$, substituting $\alpha/2$ for $\alpha$ in (-@eq-regression-ratio-uniform-projected-coverage) and inverting at zero gives the treatment-group-specific Fieller set

$$
C_{1-\alpha/2,d,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}
=
\left\{
r\in\mathbb R:
\left|
\widehat y_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-r\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right|
\leq
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/4}}{\sqrt n}
\widehat\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)
\right\}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-treatment-group-fieller-set}

Define the fitted-residual denominator standard deviations and denominator strength statistics by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\widehat\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
&=
\frac{\overline D_{1-d,n}}{\overline D_{d,n}}
\left[\widehat{\mathbf V}_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right]_{22},
\\[1ex]
T_{d,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
&=
\frac{
\sqrt n\,|\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|
}{
\widehat\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
},
\qquad
T_n^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
=
\min\left\{
T_{0,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}},
T_{1,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-denominator-strength}

As in the unadjusted construction, the set in (-@eq-regression-ratio-treatment-group-fieller-set) is a bounded interval if and only if $T_{d,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}>z_{1-\alpha/4}$.
Define the regression-adjusted Fieller difference interval by

$$
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}
=
\begin{cases}
\mathbb R,
& T_n^{z,\mathrm{reg}}\leq z_{1-\alpha/4},
\\[3ex]
\left[
\inf C_{1-\alpha/2,1,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}
-\sup C_{1-\alpha/2,0,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}},
\quad
\sup C_{1-\alpha/2,1,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}
-\inf C_{1-\alpha/2,0,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}
\right],
& T_n^{z,\mathrm{reg}}>z_{1-\alpha/4}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-fieller-difference-interval}

If an arm-specific regression or displayed standard deviation is undefined, set $C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}=\mathbb R$.
Otherwise, simultaneous coverage of the two treatment-group-specific Fieller sets implies coverage of $r_n$.
Equation (-@eq-regression-ratio-uniform-projected-coverage) and Bonferroni's inequality therefore give

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left(
r_n\in C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}
\right)
\geq
1-\alpha.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-fieller-difference-coverage}

## Delta-method interval

To construct the regression-adjusted delta-method interval, first define the population projected-outcome standard deviation by

$$
\left\{\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)\right\}^2
=
\frac{p_{1-d}}{p_d}
\begin{pmatrix}1&-r\end{pmatrix}
\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-r\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-population-projected-scale}

To obtain the corresponding matrix consistency result, premultiply $\boldsymbol u_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ by $\left(\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^{-1/2}$.
The two coordinates of the resulting vector have identity covariance.
Apply the [armwise scalar variance-consistency proof](../regression/#sec-regression-oracle-feasible-arm-variance) to these two coordinates and their sum.
Linearity of least squares gives the same transformations of the fitted residuals, polarization gives the off-diagonal entry, and fixed dimension converts entrywise convergence into operator-norm convergence.
Hence

$$
\left\|
\left(\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^{-1/2}
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\left(\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^{-1/2}
-\mathbf I_2
\right\|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-relative-residual-covariance-consistency}

Together with $\overline D_{d,n}\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}p_d$, the Rayleigh-quotient inequality therefore gives

$$
\sup_{r\in\mathbb R}
\left|
\frac{
\left\{\widehat\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)\right\}^2
}{
\left\{\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r)\right\}^2
}
-1
\right|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-uniform-projected-scale-consistency}

Define the regression-adjusted treatment-group ratio estimators and their difference by

$$
\widehat r_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{\widehat y_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}},
\qquad
\widehat r_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\widehat r_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-\widehat r_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-estimator}

These estimators are defined whenever both adjusted denominator estimates are nonzero.
Define the population score arrays and the population and feasible treatment-group-specific score standard deviations by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
&=
\frac{
u_{i,d,n}^{y,\mathrm{reg}}-r_{d,n}u_{i,d,n}^{z,\mathrm{reg}}
}{\overline z_{d,n}},
\\[1ex]
\left(\sigma_{\ell,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
&=
\frac{p_{1-d}}{p_d}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(\ell_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
\\
&=
\frac{
\left\{\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r_{d,n})\right\}^2
}{\overline z_{d,n}^2},
\\[2ex]
\widehat\sigma_{\ell,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
&=
\frac{
\widehat\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\left(\widehat r_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)
}{
\left|\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right|
}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-score-scales}

The conservative population and feasible standard deviations for the ratio difference are

$$
\widetilde\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\sigma_{\ell,0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\sigma_{\ell,1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}},
\qquad
\widehat\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\widehat\sigma_{\ell,0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
+\widehat\sigma_{\ell,1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-conservative-scales}

Also define the between-treatment-group score covariance and the relative variance by

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_{\ell,01,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
&=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_{i,0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\ell_{i,1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}},
\\[1ex]
\left(\omega_n^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
&=
\frac{
\left(\sigma_{\ell,0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
+\left(\sigma_{\ell,1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
+2s_{\ell,01,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
}{
\left(\widetilde\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
}
\leq1,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-relative-variance}

where the inequality follows from Cauchy--Schwarz.

The regression-adjusted delta-method interval is

$$
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{DM,reg}}
=
\left[
\widehat r_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
-z_{1-\alpha/2}
\frac{\widehat\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}{\sqrt n},
\widehat r_n^{\mathrm{reg}}
+z_{1-\alpha/2}
\frac{\widehat\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}{\sqrt n}
\right].
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-delta-method-interval}

As in the unadjusted case, this interval requires regular denominators.
Define the population denominator standard deviations by

$$
\left(\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2
=
\frac{p_{1-d}}{p_d}
\left[\mathbf V_{dd,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right]_{22},
\qquad d\in\{0,1\},
$$

and consider an arbitrary sequence $\boldsymbol\theta_n\in\Theta$ satisfying

$$
\min_{d\in\{0,1\}}
\frac{
\sqrt n\,|\overline z_{d,n}|
}{
\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
}
\to\infty.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-regular-denominator-condition}

Define

$$
L_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{
\widehat v_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r_{d,n})
}{\overline z_{d,n}},
\qquad
E_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
=
\frac{
\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}-\overline z_{d,n}
}{\overline z_{d,n}}.
$$

Then the regression analogue of the [exact ratio decomposition](../ratio/#sec-ratio-exact-decomposition) is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat r_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}-r_{d,n}
&=
\frac{L_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{1+E_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\\
&=
L_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
-L_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\frac{E_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{1+E_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-exact-decomposition}

For each treatment group, $L_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the regression intercept for the scalar potential outcome $(y_{i,d}-r_{d,n}z_{i,d})/\overline z_{d,n}$, whose projection residual is $\ell_{i,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}$.
The [coefficient-uniform regression normal approximation](../regression/#eq-regression-feasible-normal-approximation), applied to the difference between these two intercepts, therefore gives

$$
\frac{
\sqrt n
\left(
L_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}-L_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\right)
}{\widetilde\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
Z_n^{\mathrm{ratio,reg}},
\qquad
Z_n^{\mathrm{ratio,reg}}
\sim
N\left(0,\left(\omega_n^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2\right).
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-true-score-normal-approximation}

The same result applied to each arm separately implies

$$
\sqrt n
\frac{|L_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}|}
{\sigma_{\ell,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
=O_{\mathcal P}(1),
\qquad d\in\{0,1\}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-true-score-order}

Applying the [regression normal approximation](../regression/#eq-regression-feasible-normal-approximation) to the denominator outcome and using (-@eq-regression-ratio-regular-denominator-condition) gives

$$
\max_{d\in\{0,1\}}
\left|E_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-relative-denominator-error}

Since $\sigma_{\ell,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}/ \widetilde\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\leq1$, equations (-@eq-regression-ratio-exact-decomposition), (-@eq-regression-ratio-true-score-order), and (-@eq-regression-ratio-relative-denominator-error) imply

$$
\frac{\sqrt n}{\widetilde\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\left|
\left(\widehat r_n^{\mathrm{reg}}-r_n\right)
-
\left(L_{1,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}-L_{0,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)
\right|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-remainder-negligibility}

It remains to replace the population score scale with its feasible analogue.
The reverse triangle inequality for the covariance-induced standard deviation gives

$$
\left|
\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}
\left(\widehat r_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)
-\sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r_{d,n})
\right|
\leq
\left|\widehat r_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}-r_{d,n}\right|
\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}.
$$

Equations (-@eq-regression-ratio-exact-decomposition), (-@eq-regression-ratio-true-score-order), and (-@eq-regression-ratio-relative-denominator-error), together with (-@eq-regression-ratio-regular-denominator-condition), therefore show that the right-hand side is $o_{\mathcal P}\!\left( \sigma_{v,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}(r_{d,n}) \right)$.
Combining this fact with (-@eq-regression-ratio-uniform-projected-scale-consistency) and (-@eq-regression-ratio-relative-denominator-error) gives

$$
\max_{d\in\{0,1\}}
\left|
\frac{\widehat\sigma_{\ell,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\sigma_{\ell,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
-1
\right|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1),
\qquad
\frac{\widehat\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\widetilde\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}1.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-score-scale-consistency}

Combining (-@eq-regression-ratio-true-score-normal-approximation), (-@eq-regression-ratio-remainder-negligibility), and (-@eq-regression-ratio-score-scale-consistency), and applying the [asymptotic-equivalence perturbation](../uniform-asymptotics/#prp-asymptotic-equivalence-perturbation) and [Slutsky](../uniform-asymptotics/#prp-asymptotic-equivalence-slutsky) results yields

$$
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(\widehat r_n^{\mathrm{reg}}-r_n\right)
}{\widehat\sigma_{r,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
Z_n^{\mathrm{ratio,reg}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-feasible-normal-approximation}

Because $\left(\omega_n^{\mathrm{reg}}\right)^2\leq1$, the usual coverage argument gives, along every sequence satisfying (-@eq-regression-ratio-regular-denominator-condition),

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta_n}
\left(
r_n\in C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{DM,reg}}
\right)
\geq
1-\alpha.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-regular-delta-coverage}

## Hybrid interval

The Fieller difference interval is uniformly valid when either denominator is weak, whereas the delta-method interval is tighter when both denominators are strong.
As in the [ratio metrics note](../ratio/#hybrid-interval), choose a deterministic sequence $\tau_n$ satisfying

$$
\tau_n\to\infty,
\qquad
\frac{\tau_n}{\sqrt n}\to0,
$$

and define

$$
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{H,reg}}
=
\begin{cases}
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{DM,reg}},
& T_n^{z,\mathrm{reg}}\geq\tau_n,
\\[2ex]
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}},
& T_n^{z,\mathrm{reg}}<\tau_n.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-hybrid-interval}

The hybrid proof requires the same three ingredients as the unadjusted proof.
First, the [regression normal approximation](../regression/#eq-regression-feasible-normal-approximation) for the denominator outcome and (-@eq-regression-ratio-relative-residual-covariance-consistency) give

$$
\max_{d\in\{0,1\}}
\frac{
\sqrt n\,
\left|\widehat z_{d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}-\overline z_{d,n}\right|
}{\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
=O_{\mathcal P}(1),
\qquad
\max_{d\in\{0,1\}}
\left|
\frac{\widehat\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
{\sigma_{z,d,n}^{\mathrm{reg}}}
-1
\right|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-denominator-orders}

The triangle inequality and (-@eq-regression-ratio-denominator-orders) imply that the screen can select the delta-method interval with nonvanishing probability only along a sequence satisfying (-@eq-regression-ratio-regular-denominator-condition), exactly as in the [unadjusted screening argument](../ratio/#sec-screening-implies-regularity).
Second, the reverse triangle inequality for the covariance norm gives the same deterministic nesting threshold

$$
k_\alpha
=
\frac{
z_{1-\alpha/2}z_{1-\alpha/4}
}{
z_{1-\alpha/4}-z_{1-\alpha/2}
},
$$

and hence

$$
T_n^{z,\mathrm{reg}}\geq k_\alpha
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{DM,reg}}
\subseteq
C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{F,reg}}.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-delta-fieller-nesting}

Third, (-@eq-regression-ratio-regular-delta-coverage) controls the delta-method interval whenever the screen selects it with nonvanishing probability.
The subsequence argument used to prove the [unadjusted hybrid coverage result](../ratio/#eq-hybrid-coverage){.quarto-xref} therefore gives

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left(
r_n\in C_{1-\alpha,n}^{\mathrm{H,reg}}
\right)
\geq
1-\alpha.
$$ {#eq-regression-ratio-hybrid-coverage}

Finally, because a linear projection weakly reduces the finite-population variance of every scalar combination $y_{i,d}-rz_{i,d}$, regression adjustment weakly reduces the population conservative scale for every fixed candidate Fieller contrast and every population delta-method score relative to the unadjusted construction.
